case_info.scenario: A healthy young male patient was referred to the department of dermatology for evaluation of a solitary painful scrotal ulceration that developed rapidly 48 hours before consultation. One week before he had been diagnosed with acute tonsillitis and fever (temperature up to 38 °C), which were treated with oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. No history of a traumatic event, insect bites, genital or oral ulcers, sexual risk contacts, application of topical products, or other drug treatments was recorded. Physical examination revealed a well-circumscribed, round ulceration 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum (Figure 1A). Leukocytosis with neutrophilia was detected in an initial workup. The rest of the physical examination revealed bilateral tonsillitis and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. No inguinal lymphadenopathies were palpated. A 4-mm punch biopsy from the edge of the lesion was obtained. Representative histopathological features are shown inFigure 1B. Staining for periodic acid–Schiff, periodic acid–Schiff with diastase, and Gram failed to detect microorganisms. Immunohistochemical techniques forTreponema pallidum, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) were negative. A complete hematological and biochemical survey disclosed a moderate increase of erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein blood levels. Immunological studies, including antinuclear antibodies and both C3 and C4 proteins, were normal. Microbiological studies, including bacteriological cultures of scrotal ulcer exudates and polymerase chain reaction amplification for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, EBV, and CMV, yielded negative results. Serologic tests for syphilis, HIV, CMV, EBV, and human parvovirus B19 were negative.

case_info.caption: A, Well-circumscribed, round ulcer 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum. B, Epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: C. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Well-circumscribed, round ulcer 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum. B, Epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: C. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

case_info.explanation: C. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.caption: A, Well-circumscribed, round ulcer 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum. B, Epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: C. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

A healthy young male patient was referred to the department of dermatology for evaluation of a solitary painful scrotal ulceration that developed rapidly 48 hours before consultation. One week before he had been diagnosed with acute tonsillitis and fever (temperature up to 38 °C), which were treated with oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. Immunohistochemical techniques forTreponema pallidum, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) were negative. A complete hematological and biochemical survey disclosed a moderate increase of erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein blood levels. Immunological studies, including antinuclear antibodies and both C3 and C4 proteins, were normal. Microbiological studies, including bacteriological cultures of scrotal ulcer exudates and polymerase chain reaction amplification for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, EBV, and CMV, yielded negative results. Serologic tests for syphilis, HIV, CMV, EBV, and human parvovirus B19 were negative.

case_info.answer: Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum
case_info.caption: A, Well-circumscribed, round ulcer 15 mm in diameter with central black eschar localized on the right side of the scrotum. B, Epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: C. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum Histopathological examination revealed epidermal necrosis and a dense diffuse and interstitial neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate in the upper and middle dermis with focal abscess formation. Clear-cut signs of vasculitis were not observed in hematoxylin-eosin stains (Figure 2). A prompt clinical resolution was observed after empirical antibiotic treatment with clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Complete healing was achieved after 3 weeks of follow-up. Juvenile gangrenous vasculitis of the scrotum (JGVS) is an uncommon, distinct entity manifested by an acute onset of necrotic and painful scrotal ulceration(s) occurring exclusively in otherwise healthy young individuals often preceded and/or accompanied by a febrile episode of upper respiratory tract infection. The lesions are often solitary or few in number and correspond to sharply demarcated round to polycyclic necrotic ulcers with a central eschar. Scrotal edema has occasionally been reported,1but palpable regional lymph nodes, urinary symptoms, mucous membrane involvement, or other cutaneous lesions are not present. Acute phase reactants (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) are usually increased, whereas the other laboratory investigations are within normal ranges. JGVS is an acute, self-limiting disorder, and no association with an underlying systemic disorder has been described.2 Histopathological features are usually nonspecific. Epidermal necrosis and a dense perivascular lymphocyte or diffuse dermal neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate are observed.3In fewer than 50% of cases, fibrinoid necrosis of small blood vessel walls with extravasated erythrocytes is detected.2,4Microbiological studies usually have failed to detect a specific infectious cause.Juvenile vasculitis of the scrotumis a misleading term, and the rubric ofacute noninfectious ulcer of the scrotumprobably defines more accurately the particular and unique features of this disorder. The pathogenesis of JGVS is largely unknown. Since scrotal ulcerations appear constantly after an infectious prodrome and no further recurrences develop, a possible primary infectious disease from an unidentified microorganism could be speculated. The possibility that JGVS represents the male counterpart of the Lipschutz ulcer has been proposed.3,5,6Both disorders share many epidemiological, clinical, histopathological, and evolutive features, as well as potential associations. Some authors have also postulated that JGVS could represent a particular variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, since both disorders share similar histopathological features and neutrophilic-rich infiltrates.1,7However, the lack of recurrences and association with systemic disorders make this possibility unlikely. The diagnosis is usually established based on the characteristic clinicopathological features, age of onset, and previous upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy is only performed in selected cases to rule out other possible diagnoses. The most noteworthy differential diagnosis is early lesions of Fournier gangrene, a rapidly spreading, aggressive, and necrotic cellulitis observed in male individuals older than 50 years with considerable comorbidities in which surgical debridement is the treatment of choice.8 There is no available standard treatment approach. The lesion(s) tend to resolve spontaneously or after treatment in 2 or 3 weeks with scar formation. A dramatic response after a short course of low-dose systemic steroids with or without combination with systemic antibiotics has been reported.1Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and surgical excision have also been described as effective therapeutic options.2However, since the disease shows a self-limited course with spontaneous healing, the exact efficacy of these treatments remains controversial. The diagnosis of JGVS should be kept in mind whenever healthy young patients present with abrupt scrotal ulcerations.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
